questions.stem: What do the arrows on a food chain diagram show?

options.text: The flow of energy between trophic levels
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The direction animals face while hunting
options.explanation: Arrows track energy, not gaze.

options.text: The movement of water through soil
options.explanation: Water is not what the arrows trace.

options.text: The age of each organism
options.explanation: Age plays no role in arrow direction.

questions.stem: Why must every food chain begin with a producer?

options.text: Because producers decay fastest
options.explanation: Decay speed is irrelevant to starting a chain.

options.text: Because producers convert light energy into chemical energy that other organisms can use
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Because producers are the largest organisms
options.explanation: Size is not the reason; energy conversion is.

options.text: Because consumers cannot survive without sunlight directly
options.explanation: Consumers need food, not direct sunlight.

questions.stem: In the chain grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, eagle, which organism is the producer?

options.text: The frog, which sits mid-chain
options.explanation: Mid-chain predators are consumers.

options.text: The eagle at the top
options.explanation: Top predators are consumers, never the producer.

options.text: The grass
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The grasshopper, which eats first
options.explanation: Eating plants makes it a primary consumer, not a producer.

questions.stem: Which direction does energy travel in the chain grass to vole to owl?

options.text: From owl to vole to grass
options.explanation: Energy flows from eaten to eater, not backwards.

options.text: From the air into every organism equally
options.explanation: Air does not feed the chain.

options.text: Back and forth between all three
options.explanation: Energy does not shuttle back and forth.

options.text: From grass to vole to owl, following the feeding steps
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: A student draws an arrow from the eagle back to the grass in a food chain. Why is this wrong?

options.text: Energy cannot flow backwards because grass does not eat eagles
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Arrows must always point upwards on the page
options.explanation: Direction on the page is irrelevant; feeding direction matters.

options.text: The eagle is too large to arrow
options.explanation: Size does not block an arrow; diet does.

options.text: Arrows only belong in food webs
options.explanation: Food chains use arrows too.

questions.stem: State what food chains show.
questions.modelAnswer: Food chains show the flow of energy between organisms in an ecosystem through feeding.

questions.stem: Name the kind of organism that every food chain starts with.
questions.modelAnswer: Every food chain starts with a producer that converts light energy into chemical energy.

questions.stem: Explain why a food chain cannot begin with a fox or a rabbit.
questions.modelAnswer: A chain cannot begin with a fox or rabbit because neither converts light energy into chemical energy, so only a producer such as a plant can open the chain.

questions.stem: A pond chain opens with algae followed by snails and then fish. Identify each role.
questions.modelAnswer: Algae is the producer, snails are primary consumers feeding on it, and fish are secondary consumers eating the snails.

questions.stem: A food web is built from which structures within an ecosystem?

options.text: Random arrows with no meaning
options.explanation: Every arrow in a web traces a feeding link.

options.text: Many interconnected food chains
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: A single straight chain
options.explanation: One chain is not a web.

options.text: Circles of decomposers only
options.explanation: Webs include feeding at every level, not just decay.

questions.stem: In a web, a fox eats rabbits and also eats mice. What does this show about the fox?

options.text: It can only hold one trophic level
options.explanation: Webs allow several levels for one organism.

options.text: It breaks the rules of a food web
options.explanation: Multiple links are exactly what webs allow.

options.text: It occupies different feeding positions within the same web
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: It must be a producer in one of the chains
options.explanation: Foxes never make their own food.

questions.stem: Rabbits decline sharply in a web where foxes also eat mice and frogs eat caterpillars. Which effect follows?

options.text: Foxes vanish at once
options.explanation: Decline is gradual; foxes switch prey first.

options.text: Grass disappears immediately
options.explanation: Less grazing usually lets grass increase.

options.text: Nothing changes anywhere
options.explanation: Webs propagate change; nothing stays isolated.

options.text: Foxes eat more of their other prey, pressuring those populations
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: Why do examiners prefer answers saying populations increase or decrease rather than die out?

options.text: Because partial links usually remain, so populations shift rather than vanish
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Because extinction is illegal to write
options.explanation: It is a biological judgement, not a rule of law.

options.text: Because all animals are protected
options.explanation: Protection is not the reason; food alternatives are.

options.text: Because webs never change
options.explanation: Webs change constantly; the point is populations rarely hit zero.

questions.stem: A web shows grass, caterpillars, earthworms, frogs, mice, rabbits, foxes and hawks. Rabbit numbers fall. What happens to the grass?

options.text: Grass turns into a new species
options.explanation: Species do not transform in a web.

options.text: Grass growth increases because fewer rabbits feed on it
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Grass declines with the rabbits
options.explanation: Less feeding means more grass, not less.

options.text: Grass stays frozen at the same amount
options.explanation: Released grazing pressure shifts growth upward.

questions.stem: State what food webs are made of.
questions.modelAnswer: A food web is a network of interconnected food chains within an ecosystem.

questions.stem: State one effect of a decrease in the rabbit population on the fox population in a food web.
questions.modelAnswer: A decrease in rabbits reduces the food available to foxes, so the fox population decreases.

questions.stem: Explain why one organism can hold several trophic levels in a food web.
questions.modelAnswer: One organism holds several trophic levels because it feeds in different chains, acting as a secondary consumer in one and a tertiary consumer in another.

questions.stem: In a web, caterpillars and earthworms increase after rabbits decline. Explain the link.
questions.modelAnswer: With fewer rabbits, more grass survives, so caterpillars and earthworms gain extra plant food and their populations increase.

questions.stem: What does the width of a bar in a pyramid of numbers show?

options.text: The energy stored in each animal
options.explanation: Energy bars belong to energy pyramids.

options.text: The height each organism reaches
options.explanation: Physical height is never plotted.

options.text: The number of organisms at that trophic level
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The mass of living tissue
options.explanation: Mass belongs to biomass pyramids, not number pyramids.

questions.stem: In the grass, vole, owl pyramid of numbers, which bar is narrowest?

options.text: The grass bar
options.explanation: Grass is numerous, so its bar is wide.

options.text: The vole bar
options.explanation: Voles outnumber owls in such a chain.

options.text: All bars match
options.explanation: Counts differ, so widths differ.

options.text: The owl bar, because only one owl is counted
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: Oak tree, caterpillar, robin, woodpecker — why can the pyramid of numbers look inverted?

options.text: Because one huge oak feeds many small caterpillars, so the counts rise along the chain
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Because woodpeckers outnumber trees in nature
options.explanation: They do not; the oak is a single giant producer.

options.text: Because counting is always inaccurate
options.explanation: The shape reflects real counts, not error.

options.text: Because pyramids must invert by rule
options.explanation: No rule forces inversion; the sizes of organisms do.

questions.stem: Which pyramid type can take any shape?

options.text: None, all pyramids match one shape
options.explanation: Numbers pyramids break the standard shape.

options.text: A pyramid of numbers
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: A pyramid of biomass
options.explanation: Biomass pyramids are always pyramid shaped.

options.text: A pyramid of energy
options.explanation: Energy pyramids are always pyramid shaped.

questions.stem: Oak tree, caterpillar, robin, woodpecker — which pyramid of numbers statement is true?

options.text: All four bars match in width
options.explanation: Counts differ at every level, so widths differ.

options.text: The caterpillar bar is narrower than the oak bar
options.explanation: Many caterpillars feed on one oak, so their bar is wider.

options.text: The oak bar is narrowest because a single tree is counted
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The woodpecker bar is the widest
options.explanation: Top predators are fewest, so their bar is narrow.

questions.stem: State what a pyramid of numbers displays.
questions.modelAnswer: A pyramid of numbers displays the count of organisms living at each level of a food chain.

questions.stem: State the shape of a pyramid of numbers when many small animals feed on one large tree.
questions.modelAnswer: The pyramid of numbers is not pyramid shaped, because the count rises from one tree to many small feeders.

questions.stem: Explain why the bar for one oak tree can be narrower than the caterpillar bar above it.
questions.modelAnswer: The oak bar is narrow because a pyramid of numbers counts organisms, and a single large oak is just one organism while the caterpillars feeding on it are many.

questions.stem: A daisy patch feeds hundreds of aphids, which feed a few ladybirds. Sketch the expected shape.
questions.modelAnswer: The daisy bar is narrowest if counted as few plants, the aphid bar is widest, and the ladybird bar narrows again, giving an irregular shape rather than a clean pyramid.

questions.stem: What does a pyramid of biomass measure at each level?

options.text: The count of individual animals
options.explanation: Counting is the job of a pyramid of numbers.

options.text: The energy trapped in sunlight
options.explanation: Sunlight energy is not plotted in biomass pyramids.

options.text: The area each species covers
options.explanation: Area covered is not a biomass measure.

options.text: The mass of living organisms present
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

questions.stem: Why are pyramids of biomass always pyramid shaped?

options.text: Because available biomass always decreases towards higher trophic levels
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Because large animals always outnumber small ones
options.explanation: They usually do not; biomass still shrinks.

options.text: Because drawing conventions forbid other shapes
options.explanation: Convention follows reality; the decrease causes the shape.

options.text: Because producers weigh less than consumers
options.explanation: Producers carry the most biomass, not the least.

questions.stem: What does a pyramid of energy record?

options.text: The speed of each animal
options.explanation: Speed is not a pyramid unit.

options.text: The stored energy held inside the biomass on every trophic level
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The total number of Joules in the Sun
options.explanation: Solar output is not plotted in these pyramids.

options.text: The mass of water in each organism
options.explanation: Water content is irrelevant here.

questions.stem: Which two conventions apply when drawing any food pyramid?

options.text: Producers sit at the top
options.explanation: Producers always sit at the bottom.

options.text: Colour must match organism size
options.explanation: Colour is not part of the convention.

options.text: Bars share the same height and each bar is labelled with its trophic level
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Bars grow taller at each level
options.explanation: Bar height stays constant; width carries the data.

questions.stem: Grass carries 10,000 units of energy and the wolf at the top carries 10. What explains the drop?

options.text: Wolves store energy more efficiently than grass
options.explanation: The loss between levels, not efficiency, causes the drop.

options.text: Energy disappears into the soil and never reappears
options.explanation: Energy leaves mainly as heat and waste, not soil storage.

options.text: Grass energy was measured wrongly
options.explanation: The pattern is real and expected, not a measurement error.

options.text: Energy is lost at each trophic level, so only a fraction reaches the next
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

questions.stem: State what biomass means.
questions.modelAnswer: Biomass is the mass of living matter in the organisms at a trophic level.

questions.stem: Name the two pyramid types that are always pyramid shaped.
questions.modelAnswer: Pyramids of biomass and pyramids of energy are always pyramid shaped.

questions.stem: Explain why a pyramid of energy can never invert, unlike a pyramid of numbers.
questions.modelAnswer: A pyramid of energy can never invert because energy is lost at every feeding step, so each higher level must hold less stored energy than the level below it.

questions.stem: A student draws an energy pyramid with a wider tertiary bar than the secondary bar. Correct it.
questions.modelAnswer: The drawing is wrong because stored energy must fall at each step, so the tertiary bar must be narrower than the secondary bar beneath it.
